fieldFixes.summary: The Robots Exclusion Protocol - the robots.txt convention that Martijn Koster defined in 1994 and that crawlers had followed informally ever since - was published as Standards Track RFC 9309 in September 2022, authored by Koster and three co-authors from Google (Gary Illyes, Henner Zeller and Lizzi Sassman). It specifies rules that 'crawlers are requested to honor' and states plainly that these rules 'are not a form of access authorization'.
fieldFixes.significance: One of the web's oldest machine-readable preference signals was standardised on the eve of generative AI - a publisher-side, request-only signal that later AI-era schemes would extend, and that no individual can use to state terms about themselves.

fieldFixes.summary: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, signed on 13 June 2024 and published in the Official Journal on 12 July 2024, entered into force on 1 August 2024, twenty days after publication. As enacted, its obligations were phased: prohibitions and AI-literacy duties from 2 February 2025, general-purpose AI rules from 2 August 2025, most other provisions from 2 August 2026 and some high-risk rules from 2 August 2027. A 2026 amendment, the 'AI Omnibus' (in force 27 July 2026), then pushed the high-risk rules back to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028.
fieldFixes.significance: It began the clock on the world's first comprehensive AI law, whose copyright hook requires general-purpose AI providers to find and honour rights-holders' text-and-data-mining reservations 'including through state-of-the-art technologies' - a machine-read opt-out for works, not for people.
